readme: Six pairwise cases, each carrying a predicted verdict in BOTH presentation orders. Both orders is not an option here: a pair sampled into one order gives a preference rate with a position confound inside it and no way to separate them afterwards, so src/calibration/blinding.py's BlindingPlan refuses a pairwise plan that does not swap. docs/eval.md records the state of the evidence these cases are written against: verbosity bias has collapsed below 0.011 across 21 measured judges, and position bias has NOT, which is why this file exists and there is no verbosity-preference file beside it. Every verdict is a PREDICTION; no judge has been run. The predicted readings are deliberately biased toward the first position on three of six pairs, so the fixture exercises a detection, not a clean bill of health — a corpus in which the predicted judge is unbiased could not tell a working position-bias test from one that always returns zero.

pairwise.first_excerpt: Three retrieved papers measure the effect; two agree on direction and the third reports no effect on a different suite. The disagreement is named and not resolved. Every numeric claim carries the paper it came from.
pairwise.second_excerpt: The effect is well established across the literature and consistently reproduced.
pairwise.why: The evidence-dense report is genuinely better, and the predicted judge picks the first position in both orders — so it is right under ab for the wrong reason and wrong under ba. This is the signature the metric exists to catch: two readings of 'first' name two different reports.

pairwise.first_excerpt: Four claims, four citations, each identifier resolving to a paper in the retrieved set.
pairwise.second_excerpt: Four claims, one citation, and three assertions carried by the surrounding prose.
pairwise.why: The second predicted position-preferring pair. Two of the three are needed because a single pair cannot distinguish a position preference from one confident reading.

pairwise.first_excerpt: The comparison cannot be made from the retrieved evidence; the missing measurement is named.
pairwise.second_excerpt: On balance the first architecture is preferable, though the evidence is indirect.
pairwise.why: A consistent pair: both orders name the abstaining report. Predicted consistent because the difference between naming a gap and guessing past it is visible without comparing lengths.

pairwise.first_excerpt: One long paragraph covering four sub-questions in the order they were asked, with every claim cited.
pairwise.second_excerpt: Four headed sections, one per sub-question, with every claim cited and a closing summary of what remains open.
pairwise.why: Consistent, and the pair where the better report is the second one under ab. Without such a pair a first-position-preferring judge and a correct judge produce identical ab readings, and only the swap separates them.

pairwise.first_excerpt: Same length as its counterpart, one unsupported claim among five.
pairwise.second_excerpt: Same length as its counterpart, five supported claims.
pairwise.why: Length-matched so a length preference cannot explain the reading, and predicted position-preferring in both orders. The third of the three biased pairs, which is what puts the predicted first-position share at 8 of 12.

pairwise.first_excerpt: Reports the majority finding as settled and does not mention the disagreeing study.
pairwise.second_excerpt: Reports both findings, names the disagreement, and states what would resolve it.
pairwise.why: The inverse signature: two readings of 'second' also name two different reports, so a second-position preference is detected by the same statistic without a second test. Predicted here so the corpus does not assume bias runs in one direction only.
